column1: # Worked-example rollout verdicts for packages that carry NO tags (@PLN141).
# Hand-written, one row per package:  package <TAB> exempt|deferred <TAB> reason
# exempt   — no function here teaches more from a call site than from its signature.
# deferred — one DOES owe an example, but not in this pass; the reason names what
#            unblocks it, and the monthly by-hand review (LIBRARY_DOC_REVIEW.md) is
#            where it returns.
# A package that is neither tagged nor listed here is TODO and holds the repo's PR.
# Read the current state with, from a loft checkout:
#   make examples-progress REPO=../loft-libs-world
# NOTHING HERE IS `exempt`.  This is the largest repo in the ecosystem — fourteen
# packages, ~478 public functions — and it is geometry, which is the tier where a
# call site teaches most.  The first pass took the tier-1 package (`hex_grid`, the
# convention every other one is expressed in) and `hex_world`; `hex_form` (Phase E row 1)
# and `hex_place` (row 2) followed.  The ten rows below say what their examples would
# teach, so the next pass starts from a list rather than from a re-read.
# package
hex_body
column3: A body is a RIG — bones and joint limits — never a pose, and the pose is COMPUTED from the current rig. That is the contract a caller gets wrong, and showing it needs a rig small enough to hand-compute a world frame for. Unblocked by picking that rig; 0.3.0 made the frame checkable (rig_world_seg3 was discarding it).

column1: hex_draw
column3: The contract worth showing is the inverse read: a wall's analytic surface recovered as the exact average of its stored edges, so a wall renders as ONE flat quad rather than a strip. Needs a drawn Plan to demonstrate, so it follows hex_fit and hex_form rather than leading them.

column1: hex_edge
column3: The example is already written as prose — the sweep_path resting-position trap from moros#10, now in this package's README: a caller must not come to rest exactly at the fraction returned, because that point is on the bisector and the next hex_at may round to the far side. Turning it into a tagged test is blocked on the design question the note ends with, which is the owner's: whether a sweep_path_skin belongs here or every caller keeps its own.

column1: hex_field
column3: The largest surface in the repo (82 public functions) and the one with a real oracle — it must reproduce the Python's golden JSON byte for byte, which is possible only because the whole representation is INTEGER. That exactness is what an example should teach. Unblocked by choosing which golden fixture is small enough to read in a test.

column1: hex_fit
column3: A stencil description that carries linework, and a round trip that notices when it does not survive. The round trip is the contract; it is only readable once the canonical TEXT a stencil round-trips through is itself demonstrated, so this follows hex_form.

column1: hex_recover
column3: Law F is injectivity, and its coverage is a MEASUREMENT over an admitted space — a census, which is a long-running test rather than a teaching one. Unblocked by deciding what a fast readable subset of that census looks like.

column1: hex_roof
column3: One mechanism, several profiles: every roof form is the same function of a DISTANCE, and only the distance SOURCE changes. Which source a profile reads is the thing a caller gets wrong. Small surface (15 functions); nothing blocks it but a pass.

column1: hex_shape
column3: From a run of slots marked ROUNDED, are the centre and radius recoverable EXACTLY or only as a fit? The file says the answer is split, and a split answer is precisely what a signature cannot carry. Nothing blocks it but a pass.

column1: hex_terrain
column3: HXT is registered. The contract is the scale boundary — a coarse overland cell is hundreds of metres and is the terrain AUTHORITY, while the walked world is fine — so the trap is a coordinate crossing it. Unblocked by choosing a terrain fixture small enough to assert against.

column1: hex_way
column3: A way is authored as ONE exact centreline and every other line is an OFFSET of it; that is what escapes the hex quantisation floor, which bottoms out around half a hex. The floor is the number a caller needs and no signature carries it. Nothing blocks it but a pass.
